track.name: Accessibility
track.blurb: Accessibility interview questions for frontend roles: WCAG 2.2, ARIA and the accessibility tree, keyboard and focus, forms, live regions, testing and component patterns.

questions.q: What is WCAG, what do the POUR principles mean, and which conformance level should a product target?
questions.answer:
**WCAG is the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines; 2.2 is the current version. It groups testable success criteria under four principles: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. Each criterion is Level A, AA or AAA, and products should target WCAG 2.2 AA, because AA is what laws, contracts and procurement rules reference.**

## The structure
```text
4 principles -> 13 guidelines -> success criteria (A / AA / AAA)
                                  + Understanding docs + Techniques
```
The success criteria are the normative, testable part. The "Understanding" documents explain intent and edge cases and are what you cite when a design decision is disputed.

## POUR with real criteria
- **Perceivable**: information is not invisible to all of someone's senses. Text alternatives for images (1.1.1, A), captions for prerecorded video (1.2.2, A), structure in markup not just visually (1.3.1, A), text contrast 4.5:1 (1.4.3, AA), reflow at 320 CSS px width (1.4.10, AA).
- **Operable**: everything works with a keyboard (2.1.1, A), no keyboard traps (2.1.2, A), skip repeated blocks (2.4.1, A), visible focus (2.4.7, AA), pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS px (2.5.8, AA, new in 2.2).
- **Understandable**: page language set (3.1.1, A), no surprise context changes on focus (3.2.1, A), labels or instructions (3.3.2, A), errors identified in text (3.3.1, A) with suggestions (3.3.3, AA).
- **Robust**: every control exposes name, role and state to assistive technology (4.1.2, A); status messages announced without moving focus (4.1.3, AA).

## Levels
- **A**: failures block users completely (no keyboard access, unlabelled controls).
- **AA**: the commonly required level. The EU Accessibility Act (through EN 301 549), Section 508 (2.0 AA), the 2024 ADA Title II rule (2.1 AA) and most enterprise contracts point here.
- **AAA**: stricter (7:1 contrast, no timing at all, sign language). W3C states it is not recommended as a general policy for entire sites because some content cannot satisfy it. Teams adopt individual AAA criteria where cheap, like larger touch targets.

Conformance is per page and per complete process: a checkout conforms only if every step does.

## How I would phrase the target
"We target WCAG 2.2 AA for all new work. That is a superset of 2.1 AA, which is what most regulation cites, so it covers us legally and adds the 2.2 criteria that matter in practice: target size, focus not hidden by sticky headers, dragging alternatives and accessible authentication."

WCAG 3 exists only as a working draft with a different scoring model; nothing legal references it yet.
followUps: Why is AAA not recommended as a blanket target?
Give an example success criterion for each principle.
Is WCAG 3 something you would design to today?
mistakes: Weak answers recite the acronym but cannot name a single concrete success criterion or number like 4.5:1.
Weak answers say "AAA to be safe" without knowing W3C advises against AAA for whole sites.
Weak answers treat WCAG as screen reader support only and forget keyboard, zoom, motion and cognitive needs.

questions.q: What changed in WCAG 2.2 compared with 2.1?
questions.answer:
**WCAG 2.2 (a W3C Recommendation since October 2023) added nine success criteria and removed one, 4.1.1 Parsing. The ones that affect most products at AA are Focus Not Obscured, Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum) and Accessible Authentication, plus two Level A criteria: Consistent Help and Redundant Entry.**

## The additions
| Criterion | Level | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | AA | A focused element must not be completely hidden by author content: sticky headers, cookie banners, chat widgets. Fix with `scroll-padding-top`, non-overlapping layouts, dismissible banners. |
| 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | AAA | No part of the focused element is hidden. |
| 2.4.13 Focus Appearance | AAA | Focus indicator of a minimum area (like a 2 CSS px perimeter) with 3:1 contrast between states. |
| 2.5.7 Dragging Movements | AA | Anything done by dragging also works with single-pointer actions without dragging: move up/down buttons on a sortable list, click-to-place on a map, tap on a slider track. Keyboard support alone does not satisfy it; it is about pointer users who cannot drag. |
| 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) | AA | Pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS px, or spaced so a 24 px circle around each does not overlap another. Exceptions: inline links in text, user-agent controls, essential presentation. |
| 3.2.6 Consistent Help | A | If help mechanisms exist (contact details, chat, FAQ link), they appear in the same relative order across pages. |
| 3.3.7 Redundant Entry | A | Information already entered in a process is auto-populated or selectable rather than re-typed (e.g. "billing same as shipping"), except for security or when it is essential. |
| 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | AA | No cognitive function test (remembering a password, transcribing a code, solving a puzzle) unless there is an alternative, a mechanism to help (allowing paste and password managers), or it is object/personal-content recognition. |
| 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) | AAA | Removes the object and personal-content recognition exceptions. |

## The removal
4.1.1 Parsing required well-formed markup (no duplicate attributes, proper nesting). Browsers and assistive tech now build accessibility trees robustly from imperfect HTML, and the real-world problems it caught are covered by other criteria (4.1.2 for broken names and roles, 1.3.1 for relationships). For 2.1 audits it is treated as always satisfied.

## Practical impact on a typical app
- Audit icon buttons, close buttons and dense tables for 24 px targets.
- Check that sticky headers do not cover focused fields when tabbing backwards.
- Give drag-and-drop boards a non-drag move action (menu: "Move to column...").
- Never block paste on password or OTP fields; set `autocomplete` correctly so password managers work; offer passkeys or magic links.
- Persist entered data across multi-step forms.

2.2 is backwards compatible: meeting 2.2 AA means meeting 2.1 AA and 2.0 AA.
followUps: How would you pass Accessible Authentication with a password login?
What does Dragging Movements mean for a sortable list?
Why was 4.1.1 Parsing removed?
mistakes: Weak answers cannot name more than one new criterion or confuse 2.5.8 (24 px, AA) with 2.5.5 (44 px, AAA).
Weak answers assume 2.2 is a breaking change; it is backwards compatible with 2.1.

questions.q: Why does accessibility matter to a business beyond doing the right thing?
questions.answer:
**Accessibility affects revenue, legal exposure, sales eligibility and product quality. Disabled people are a large market, inaccessible flows lose them at checkout, regulators and courts expect WCAG AA, enterprise and public-sector buyers require a conformance report before purchase, and the same work improves usability, SEO and code quality for everyone.**

## The arguments, with substance
**Market size.** The WHO estimates around 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six, live with a significant disability, and many more have age-related vision, hearing or dexterity decline. Add temporary and situational limitations (a broken arm, bright sunlight, a muted video on a train). An inaccessible checkout is a conversion bug for all of them.

**Legal and regulatory risk.**
- US: courts have treated inaccessible websites of public-facing businesses as ADA violations, and thousands of web accessibility suits are filed each year, often against retail and hospitality sites. The 2024 DOJ Title II rule requires WCAG 2.1 AA for state and local government. Section 508 covers federal agencies and vendors.
- EU: the European Accessibility Act has applied since 28 June 2025 to e-commerce, banking, transport ticketing, e-books and more, through EN 301 549 (aligned with WCAG 2.1 AA).
- Settlements typically require remediation, monitoring and fees, which cost far more than building it in.

**Sales eligibility.** B2B and government buyers ask for an Accessibility Conformance Report (usually based on the ITI VPAT template). Without a credible one, you are excluded from RFPs. This is often the argument that moves leadership fastest.

**Quality and cost.** Accessible components are better components: semantic HTML, real buttons and labelled forms make tests more robust (role-based queries), improve SEO (headings, alt text, link text), support voice assistants and automation, and reduce custom JS. Retrofitting after launch costs many times more than building it into the design system.

**Brand and talent.** Public accessibility failures generate bad press; engineers increasingly expect it as a quality bar.

## How I would turn this into a programme
1. Commit to WCAG 2.2 AA, publish an accessibility statement with a feedback channel.
2. Fix at the source: accessible design tokens and components (or a vetted headless library) so product teams inherit compliance.
3. Shift left: lint (jsx-a11y), axe in CI, keyboard and screen reader checks in the definition of done.
4. Prioritise the backlog by user impact on critical journeys (sign-up, checkout, core task), not by raw violation count.
5. Periodic external audits for the ACR; occasional usability sessions with disabled users.

**On overlays:** one-line "AI accessibility" widgets do not fix underlying semantics, are criticised by many disabled users, and have not stopped lawsuits. I would not use one as a compliance strategy.
followUps: How would you prioritise a large backlog of accessibility issues?
What is a VPAT or ACR?
What do you think of accessibility overlay products?
mistakes: Weak answers only cite morality or only cite lawsuits, without market, quality and procurement arguments.
Weak answers propose an overlay script as a quick fix.
Weak answers treat accessibility as a one-off audit instead of a process.

questions.q: What is the first rule of ARIA, and when is ARIA actually the right tool?
questions.answer:
**The first rule of ARIA is: if a native HTML element or attribute already has the semantics and behaviour you need, use it instead of adding ARIA to a generic element. ARIA only changes what assistive technology is told; it adds no focus, keyboard handling or behaviour. It is the right tool for widgets HTML lacks, for relationships HTML cannot express, and for live announcements.**

## Why native wins
A `<button>` gives you, for free: the button role, focusability, Enter and Space activation (Space on keyup), form submission, the `disabled` state, correct behaviour in Windows forced-colours mode, and consistent support across every browser and screen reader.

`<div role="button">` gives you only the role. To match the native element you must add `tabIndex={0}`, Enter and Space key handlers with the right event timing, `aria-disabled` handling, focus styles, and you still do not get form submission. Every one of those is a promise the role makes to a screen reader user; failing to keep it is worse than not making it.

## The five rules from the W3C "Using ARIA" note
1. Prefer native HTML.
2. Do not change native semantics unless you must (`<h2 role="tab">` is wrong; put a button inside the heading).
3. All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable.
4. Never use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on a focusable element.
5. All interactive elements must have an accessible name.

## When ARIA is right
- **Composite widgets with no native equivalent**: tabs (`tablist`, `tab`, `tabpanel`), tree views, comboboxes with custom listboxes, application menus, grids. Follow the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide pattern for roles, states and keyboard model.
- **States native HTML cannot express**: `aria-expanded` on a disclosure button, `aria-pressed` on a toggle, `aria-current="page"` in navigation, `aria-invalid` on a field after validation.
- **Relationships**: `aria-describedby` for hints and errors, `aria-labelledby` to build a name from visible text ("Remove, Wireless headphones"), `aria-controls`.
- **Live regions**: `role="status"`, `role="alert"`, `aria-live` for announcing changes.
- **Hiding duplicates**: `aria-hidden="true"` on a decorative icon next to text.

## The data point
WebAIM's annual analysis of the top million home pages consistently finds that pages using ARIA have more detected accessibility errors on average than pages without it. ARIA is not the cause on its own; it correlates with custom widgets built without the keyboard behaviour and state management the roles promise. Hence the community shorthand: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

## How I apply it
Start with semantic HTML, reach for a native element even if it needs styling work (`appearance: none`, `accent-color`), then a well-tested headless library for complex widgets, and only then hand-written ARIA, tested with a screen reader.
followUps: What else must you implement if you use role="button" on a div?
What are the other rules of ARIA use?
Why do pages with more ARIA tend to have more errors?
mistakes: Weak answers think ARIA adds keyboard behaviour or focusability.
Weak answers sprinkle aria-label everywhere as "doing accessibility".
Weak answers cannot name a legitimate use case such as tabs, combobox or aria-describedby.

questions.q: How does the browser compute an element's accessible name?
questions.answer:
**The browser follows the W3C Accessible Name and Description Computation spec. Simplified, it takes the first source that yields text: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native labelling (label element, alt, caption, legend), then the element's text content for roles that allow naming from content, and finally title or placeholder as a weak fallback.**

## The order
```text
1. aria-labelledby  -> concatenated text of referenced ids, in order
                       (works even if the referenced nodes are hidden)
2. aria-label       -> the attribute string
3. native label     -> <label for>/wrapping label for inputs,
                       alt for images, <caption> for tables,
                       <legend> for fieldsets, value for input type=submit
4. content          -> descendant text, only for roles that allow it:
                       button, link, heading, tab, option, menuitem, cell...
5. title / placeholder -> last resort, poorly supported as a name
```

## Consequences worth knowing
- **Overrides are total.** `<button aria-label="Close dialog">Cancel</button>` is announced "Close dialog". A voice control user who says "click Cancel" fails. WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name (A) requires the visible label text to be part of the accessible name; best practice is to start with it.
- **Generic elements cannot be named.** `div` and `span` have the `generic` role, which prohibits naming in ARIA 1.2. `<div aria-label="Revenue chart">` is ignored by many screen readers. Give it a role that supports names (`role="img"`, `role="region"`, `role="group"`) or use visible text.
- **Name from content explains empty links.** An `<a>` containing only an SVG icon has no name unless the SVG is labelled or there is visually hidden text. WebAIM's Million report lists empty links and buttons among the most common failures.
- **aria-labelledby composes.** `aria-labelledby="btn-remove item-title"` produces "Remove Wireless headphones" from two visible strings, which is better than a hard-coded string that can drift from the UI.
- **Hidden text can be referenced.** `aria-labelledby` can point at a `hidden` element, which is handy but also hides the name from sighted users, so use it sparingly.

## Descriptions are separate
`aria-describedby` (and native sources such as a table's caption in some cases) produces the **description**, announced after name, role and state, often after a pause. Use it for hints and error messages: "Password, secure edit text, required, At least 12 characters".

## How to check
Chrome DevTools Accessibility pane shows the computed name and which source contributed it, with overridden sources struck through. Testing Library's `getByRole("button", { name: "Delete invoice" })` and `toHaveAccessibleName` assert it in tests.

## Rule of thumb
Visible label first, native association second, `aria-labelledby` to reuse visible text, `aria-label` only for icon-only controls, never `title` or `placeholder` as the name.
followUps: Why does aria-label on a plain div often not work?
What is Label in Name and why does it matter for voice control?
How is a description different from a name?
mistakes: Weak answers think placeholder or title are reliable names.
Weak answers do not know aria-labelledby takes precedence over aria-label.
Weak answers override visible text with a different aria-label, breaking voice control.

questions.q: What is the accessibility tree and how do you inspect it?
questions.answer:
**The accessibility tree is a simplified parallel tree that the browser builds from the DOM and CSS, where each node has a role, an accessible name, states and properties, and a value. The browser exposes it to assistive technology through the operating system's accessibility API, so it is what a screen reader actually reads. You inspect it in the Chrome or Firefox DevTools accessibility panels.**

## How it is built
```text
DOM + computed CSS
      |
      v
Accessibility tree (role, name, description, states, value, relations)
      |
      v
Platform API: UIA / IAccessible2 (Windows), NSAccessibility (macOS),
              UIAccessibility (iOS), AT-SPI (Linux), Android accessibility
      |
      v
Screen reader, voice control, switch software, magnifier
```
Examples of mapping:
- `<button>Save</button>` becomes `button "Save"`.
- `<input type="checkbox" checked id="t"><label for="t">Terms</label>` becomes `checkbox "Terms" checked`.
- `<nav aria-label="Main">` becomes a `navigation "Main"` landmark.
- `<div class="card">` becomes `generic`, which is usually flattened away.

## What removes nodes
Removed from the tree: `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, the `hidden` attribute, `aria-hidden="true"` (and their whole subtree), and content inside an `inert` subtree.
**Not** removed: `opacity: 0`, positioning off-screen, `clip`/1px tricks. That is why the `.sr-only` class works: visually hidden, still announced. It is also why an invisible but present element can confuse screen reader users.

## How to inspect
- **Chrome DevTools**: Elements panel, Accessibility tab shows the selected node's computed role, name (and which source supplied it), description and states. You can enable the full-page accessibility tree view to browse it instead of the DOM.
- **Firefox Accessibility Inspector**: shows the tree, flags issues (contrast, keyboard, text labels) and can simulate colour vision deficiencies.
- **Safari**: the Web Inspector Node panel shows accessibility properties.
- **Playwright**: `page.accessibility` snapshots and `expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` compare a YAML representation of the tree in tests.
- **Testing Library**: `screen.getByRole` queries an approximation of the tree; `logRoles(container)` prints the roles it sees.

## Why it matters
A visually perfect page can be empty or nonsensical in the accessibility tree: a "button" that is a `div` with no role or name does not exist for a screen reader user. Inspecting the tree is the fastest first debugging step, before opening a screen reader.
followUps: Which CSS properties remove an element from the accessibility tree?
How does aria-hidden differ from display none?
Why do div and span disappear from the tree?
mistakes: Weak answers think screen readers read the DOM or the pixels directly.
Weak answers assume opacity 0 or off-screen positioning hides content from screen readers.
Weak answers never mention DevTools accessibility tooling.

questions.q: When should you use a button and when a link?
questions.answer:
**Use a link (`a` with `href`) when activating it navigates to a URL; use a button when it performs an action on the current page, such as submitting, toggling, opening a dialog or deleting. The choice is about behaviour, not appearance: style a link to look like a button if you need to, but keep the right element.** ## Why it matters | | Link | Button | | --- | --- | --- | | Role announced | "link" | "button" | | Activation keys | Enter | Enter and Space | | Browser features | Open in new tab, copy link address, middle-click, history, prefetch | Form submission (default `type="submit"` inside forms) | | Screen reader lists | Appears in the links list (NVDA+F7, VoiceOver rotor) | Appears in form controls / buttons list | | Focusable | Only with `href` | Always (unless disabled) | Screen reader users hear the role and form expectations: a "link" should take them somewhere, a "button" should do something here. Mismatches cause confusion, and keyboard behaviour differs (Space on a link scrolls the page). ## Common anti-patterns ```tsx // Not focusable, no link role, cannot open in new tab router.push("/settings")}>Settings // Navigation disguised as a button: no URL, no new tab, no prefetch // A div pretending to be either
Save
``` Fixes: ```tsx Settings {/* renders a real anchor with href */} ``` ## Edge cases - **Download**: `a href="/report.pdf" download` is a link (it retrieves a resource); a control that generates the file on click via JS is a button. - **"Load more"**: a button (action on the page); "Next page" with a URL change in a paginated list is a link. - **Opening a dialog**: button, possibly with `aria-haspopup="dialog"`. - **Buttons in forms**: set `type="button"` on buttons that should not submit; the default type is submit. - **Links styled as buttons** for call-to-action ("Start free trial") are fine; keep the link role. ## In practice In React, lint with `jsx-a11y/anchor-is-valid` and `jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events` to catch the anti-patterns, and in Testing Library assert `getByRole("link", { name: "Settings" })` so a regression to a div fails the test.
followUps: What is wrong with an anchor that has no href and an onClick?
How should a Next.js Link that also tracks analytics be marked up?
Should a "Download PDF" control be a link or a button?
mistakes: Weak answers choose by appearance ("it looks like a button").
Weak answers use anchors without href or buttons that call router.push for ordinary navigation.
Weak answers ignore the different keyboard activation (Space for buttons).

questions.q: How do you handle focus when a modal dialog opens and closes?
questions.answer:
**On open, move focus into the dialog; while it is open, keep Tab cycling inside it, make the rest of the page inert and let Escape close it; on close, return focus to the element that opened it. The native `dialog` element with `showModal()` does most of this, and the dialog needs an accessible name via `aria-labelledby` pointing at its heading.** ## The contract (from the ARIA Authoring Practices dialog pattern) ```text open: focus -> first focusable element or the safest action (Cancel) for destructive confirms or the heading (tabindex=-1) if content is long while: Tab / Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog background inert: not focusable, not clickable, hidden from AT Escape closes close: focus -> the invoking element (or a logical fallback) ``` ## Native implementation ```tsx function DeleteDialog({ onConfirm }: { onConfirm: () => void }) { const ref = useRef(null); return ( <>

Delete this project?

All files will be removed permanently.

 ); } ``` `showModal()` renders in the top layer (no z-index wars), makes everything outside inert, handles Escape (via the `cancel` event), and the HTML spec restores focus to the previously focused element on close. `form method="dialog"` closes it with the clicked button's value. `show()` (non-modal) does none of the inerting. ## Custom overlays If you cannot use `dialog` (legacy design system, complex animations): - Render the overlay outside the app root (a portal) and set `inert` on the app root while it is open. `inert` is supported in all major browsers since 2023 and replaces the old pattern of `aria-hidden` on siblings plus a JavaScript Tab loop. - Add `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, `aria-labelledby`. - Store `document.activeElement` before opening; on close, `focus()` it if still connected, otherwise a fallback such as the list heading. - Lock page scroll behind the dialog. Libraries like Radix Dialog and React Aria's `useDialog`/`FocusScope` implement all of this. ## Details that separate good answers - **Initial focus choice**: for "Discard changes?" focus Cancel, not Discard, so an accidental Enter is harmless. Use `role="alertdialog"` for such urgent confirmations. - **Do not trap non-modal UI**: popovers, menus and disclosures should let Tab leave (and usually close). - **Screen reader browse mode** ignores focus traps, so the background must be truly inert or hidden from the tree, not just behind a visual backdrop. - **Testing**: Playwright `await page.keyboard.press("Tab")` loops and `expect(trigger).toBeFocused()` after close; manually with NVDA and VoiceOver to confirm the name is announced on open.
followUps: Where should initial focus go in a long dialog or a destructive confirmation?
What does the inert attribute do?
What if the trigger element no longer exists when the dialog closes?
mistakes: Weak answers forget to return focus to the trigger on close.
Weak answers trap focus visually but leave the background reachable by screen reader browse mode.
Weak answers do not name the dialog with aria-labelledby.

questions.q: What do tabindex values 0, -1 and positive numbers do, and when do you use each?
questions.answer:
**`tabindex="0"` adds an element to the normal Tab order at its DOM position; use it only for custom interactive widgets. `tabindex="-1"` makes an element focusable by script and click but skips it with Tab; use it for programmatic focus targets and inactive items in a roving-tabindex widget. Positive values pull elements ahead of everything else in the page and should never be used.**

## How the order is built
```text
1. tabindex > 0, in ascending numeric order     <- avoid
2. everything else focusable, in DOM order:
   a[href], button, input, select, textarea, summary,
   [contenteditable], iframe, media with controls, tabindex="0"
skipped: tabindex="-1", disabled controls, inert, display:none,
         visibility:hidden
```

## When to use each
- **No tabindex**: native interactive elements already participate. A `button` does not need `tabindex="0"`.
- **`0`**: a `div role="slider"` or other custom control you could not build natively; the active item of a roving tabindex group.
- **`-1`**:
  - The `h1` you focus after a client-side route change.
  - A `main` element targeted by a skip link, so focus truly moves.
  - An error summary you focus after a failed submit.
  - A dialog container when no child should receive initial focus.
  - The non-active items in a toolbar, tab list or menu.
- **Positive**: never. With `tabindex="3"` on one element, the page order becomes: every positive element in numeric order, then the rest. It is fragile and confuses everyone as soon as two components use it.

## Common confusion
**Making text focusable for screen readers** is unnecessary and harmful: screen readers read all content with their own virtual cursor (arrow keys, heading navigation). Focusable static content adds pointless Tab stops for keyboard users and may be announced oddly.

**Visual versus DOM order**: CSS `order`, `flex-direction: row-reverse`, grid placement and absolute positioning can make visual order differ from DOM order, so focus jumps around (2.4.3 Focus Order and 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence). Fix the DOM order, not tabindex.

**Disabled versus aria-disabled**: the `disabled` attribute removes a control from the Tab order; `aria-disabled="true"` keeps it focusable and discoverable (useful so users can find out why it is unavailable), but you must block activation yourself.

## Checking
Tab through the page with the mouse unplugged; in Chrome DevTools, Lighthouse and axe flag positive tabindex values; `jsx-a11y/tabindex-no-positive` catches them in lint.
followUps: Why should you not add tabindex="0" to headings and paragraphs for screen reader users?
How does CSS order or flex-direction affect tab order?
What makes an element natively focusable?
mistakes: Weak answers use positive tabindex to fix a visual order problem.
Weak answers make static content focusable to "help" screen reader users.
Weak answers forget tabindex="-1" for programmatic focus targets like headings and error summaries.

questions.q: How do you make form validation errors accessible?
questions.answer:
**Errors must be specific visible text next to the field, programmatically tied to it with `aria-invalid="true"` and `aria-describedby`, and easy to reach: on a failed submit, focus an error summary that links to each invalid field, or focus the first invalid field on short forms. Never signal errors with colour alone.** ## Field-level markup ```tsx

We will send your receipt here.

{error &&

Enter an email address like name@example.com

} ``` On focus a screen reader says something like "Email address, edit text, invalid entry, We will send your receipt here. Enter an email address like name@example.com". This covers 3.3.1 Error Identification (A), 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA) and 1.4.1 Use of Color (A). `aria-errormessage` is the purpose-built attribute (it is only exposed when `aria-invalid` is true), but screen reader support has historically lagged; `aria-describedby` works everywhere, and some teams set both. ## Submit-time pattern: error summary ```text +-----------------------------------------+ | There is a problem | <- div tabindex=-1, receives focus | - Enter your full name (link) | <- href="#name" | - Enter a date in the past (link) | +-----------------------------------------+ inline errors also shown beside each field ``` - Focusing the summary makes screen readers read it immediately and gives keyboard users a starting point. - Each link moves focus to the field, where the inline error is announced again. - For server-rendered pages, prefix the `title` with "Error: " so the problem is announced on load. The GOV.UK Design System's error summary and error message components are the best-documented, research-backed version of this pattern. ## Timing - Do not show errors on untouched fields or while the user is still typing a valid-so-far value. - Validate on blur and on submit; once a field is invalid, re-validate on change so the error clears as soon as it is fixed. - Async checks (username taken) go to a polite live region after a pause. ## Things to avoid - **Disabled submit until valid**: the user gets no reason, and disabled buttons are skipped by Tab. - **role="alert" on each inline error**: on submit, ten alerts fire at once and interrupt each other. - **Clearing the form** on error; values must be preserved (also 3.3.7 Redundant Entry). - **Generic messages** like "Invalid input". ## With Server Actions Return a typed field-error map from the action (validated with zod), render the same markup, keep `name` attributes so the form works without JS, and move focus to the summary in an effect when the error state changes. Progressive enhancement and accessibility reinforce each other here.

questions.q: Why is a placeholder not a substitute for a label, and how do you label form controls correctly?
questions.answer:
**A placeholder disappears as soon as the user types, is usually low contrast, is not reliably exposed as the accessible name, and is easily mistaken for a pre-filled value. Every control needs a persistent visible label that is programmatically associated, using `label for` (or a wrapping label), with `fieldset` and `legend` for groups.** ## Problems with placeholder-as-label - **Memory load**: once typing starts, the hint is gone. People with cognitive or memory disabilities, or anyone interrupted, lose track of what the field wants. Reviewing a filled form shows values without labels. - **Contrast**: default placeholder grey is usually around 3:1 or below on white; raising it makes it look like a real value. - **Accessible name**: browsers do use placeholder as a last-resort name, but support and announcement vary; it is not a reliable label. - **Looks pre-filled**: users skip fields that appear complete. - **Translation and zoom**: placeholders get truncated on narrow inputs. ## Correct labelling ```tsx // Explicit association (clicking the label focuses the input; bigger target) // Implicit association // Hint: associated, visible, placed before the field

For example, 27 3 1990

// Groups
Contact preference
``` Use `useId` to generate ids in React so repeated components do not collide. ## When aria-label is acceptable For a single obvious field where a visible label would be redundant, like a search box next to a "Search" button, `aria-label="Search"` is acceptable. Even then a visible label helps more people. Never use `aria-label` that differs from visible text (voice control users say what they see: 2.5.3 Label in Name). ## Floating labels A label that starts inside the field and moves above on focus can be accessible if it is a real `label` element, stays visible after typing, keeps sufficient contrast and size in both positions, and does not overlap the value at high zoom. Many implementations fail one of these; a static label above the field is simpler and tests better. ## Checking DevTools accessibility pane shows each input's computed name; `getByLabelText("City")` in Testing Library fails if association is broken; axe flags inputs with no label (one of the most common failures in WebAIM's Million report).

questions.q: When should a form validate as the user types, and how should errors be announced?
questions.answer:
**Do not punish users while they are still typing: validate a field when they leave it (blur) and on submit, but once a field is showing an error, re-validate on every change so the error disappears the moment it is fixed. This is often summarised as "reward early, punish late". Announce through `aria-describedby` on the field and polite live regions, not assertive alerts on every keystroke.**

## The state machine
```text
untouched ----type----> dirty (no error shown)
dirty ------blur------> validate -> valid   : no message
                                   invalid : show error, aria-invalid=true
invalid ----change----> validate -> valid   : clear error immediately
                                   invalid : keep (do not re-announce)
any --------submit----> validate all -> summary or focus first error
```
Why: an email field that shouts "Invalid email" after "j" is wrong and, for a screen reader user, an interruption on every key. Clearing errors eagerly gives positive feedback exactly when the user fixes the problem.

## Announcing
- **Inline errors on blur**: render the message and reference it in `aria-describedby`. When the user returns to the field it is announced with the field. Many screen readers do not announce describedby changes while focus is elsewhere, so if immediate feedback matters, also send a short message to a polite live region ("Email: enter a valid address").
- **Submit**: focus an error summary or the first invalid field. That focus move is the announcement.
- **Async checks** (username availability): debounce (300 to 500 ms after typing stops), show a visible "Checking..." state, then a polite status: "Username available" or "Username taken". Keep the result tied to the field via `aria-describedby`.
- **Counters and strength meters**: announce at thresholds ("20 characters remaining", "Strength: strong"), not on every keystroke. `role="status"` with debounced text works well.
- **Assertive** only when something blocks the user right now (session about to expire, payment declined).

## Native validation trade-offs
`required`, `type="email"`, `pattern` and `:user-invalid` give semantics, mobile keyboards and built-in bubbles that are reasonably accessible. But messages are browser-worded, appear one at a time and cannot be styled. A common approach: keep the attributes for semantics, add `noValidate` to the form, and render your own messages using the Constraint Validation API (`input.validity`) so the logic stays native.

## Server-side reality
Client-side validation is a convenience; the server validates again (zod schema shared between client and Server Action). The server's errors must render in the same accessible structure, and the form must keep values.

## Testing
With NVDA's speech viewer open, type a bad value, tab away, come back, fix it, submit. You should hear the error once on return, silence while fixing, confirmation when valid, and a clear summary on a failed submit.

questions.q: How do you announce dynamic content changes to screen reader users?
questions.answer:
**Changes outside the user's current focus are silent to screen readers unless you act. If the user needs to act on the new content (a dialog, a new page, an error summary), move focus to it. If it is status information ("Saved", "12 results", "Added to cart"), announce it through a live region that already exists in the DOM, usually `role="status"` (polite).** ## Decision rule ```text Does the user need to do something with the new content now? yes -> move focus (dialog, error summary, new route heading) no -> announce via live region (status, results count, saved) Is it urgent and blocking (payment failed, session expiring)? yes -> role="alert" / aria-live="assertive" no -> role="status" / aria-live="polite" ``` WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) requires status messages to be programmatically exposed so assistive tech can present them without focus moving. ## A reusable announcer ```tsx export function AnnouncerProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const [msg, setMsg] = useState(""); const announce = useCallback((text: string) => { setMsg(""); // clear so identical repeats are re-read window.setTimeout(() => setMsg(text), 100); }, []); return ( {children}
{msg}
 ); } ``` Mount it once at the root (with an assertive sibling for urgent messages). Components call `announce("3 results")`. One announcer avoids duplicates and competing regions; React Aria provides the same idea as `announce()` from `@react-aria/live-announcer`. ## Rules that make it work 1. **Region exists before the change.** Screen readers register live regions when they appear; content inserted together with a new region is often missed. 2. **Change text content**, not the `aria-live` attribute. 3. **Short, self-contained messages**: "3 results for shoes", not the list itself. 4. **Debounce noisy sources**: search-as-you-type announces the count after the user pauses, not per keystroke. 5. **Do not put interactive content** in live regions. ## Real examples - Filter applied: keep focus on the filter control, announce "24 products". - Add to cart: button keeps focus, announce "Added Navy coat to cart, 3 items". - Infinite list loaded: "20 more results loaded". - Chat: the message list is `role="log"` (polite, additions only). - Copy to clipboard: "Copied" (clear and re-set so a second copy is also announced). ## Verifying NVDA's speech viewer shows a log of everything spoken; VoiceOver's caption panel does the same. Listen for missing, duplicated or interrupting announcements, and test on at least two screen readers because their queuing behaviour differs.

Weak answers render the live region at the same moment as the message.

questions.q: What is the difference between aria-live polite and assertive, and why might an announcement not fire?
questions.answer:
**`aria-live="polite"` queues the announcement until the screen reader is idle; `aria-live="assertive"` may interrupt whatever is being spoken. Use polite (or `role="status"`) by default and assertive (or `role="alert"`) only for urgent, blocking information. Announcements usually fail because the region did not exist before its content changed, it is hidden, or the text did not actually change.** ## The attributes and roles | | Behaviour | Typical use | | --- | --- | --- | | `aria-live="polite"` / `role="status"` | After current speech | Saved, results count, progress | | `aria-live="assertive"` / `role="alert"` | Interrupts | Payment failed, connection lost, session expiring | | `role="log"` | Polite, additions | Chat, activity feed | | `role="timer"`, `role="marquee"` | Off by default | Clocks, tickers | | `aria-atomic="true"` | Read the whole region, not only the changed node | "Cart: 3 items" where only the number changes | | `aria-busy="true"` | Hold announcements while the region updates | Batch updates, then set false | | `aria-relevant` | Which changes count (additions, removals, text) | Rarely needed; inconsistent support | Assertive messages that interrupt are like someone talking over you; overusing them makes an app exhausting, and they can cut off the user's own reading or typing feedback. ## Why announcements do not fire 1. **Region created with the message.** `{saved &&
Saved
}` inserts region and text together; many screen reader and browser combinations never register it. Fix: render the empty region on mount and change its text. 2. **Hidden region.** Inside `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden` or an `aria-hidden` ancestor (common when a modal hides the app root and the announcer lives in the app root). Use the `.sr-only` technique, not display none. 3. **Same text again.** Setting "Copied" when it already says "Copied" changes nothing. Clear, then set after a short delay. 4. **Attribute toggling.** Adding `aria-live` at the moment of change is unreliable. 5. **Focus moved at the same time.** A focus change announcement can supersede the live message; sequence them or pick one. 6. **Too fast or too many.** Rapid successive updates get collapsed; debounce and send the final state. 7. **Platform quirks.** VoiceOver on iOS is particularly sensitive to late-added regions; test there. ## Debugging approach Inspect the node in DevTools (live region properties appear in the accessibility pane), confirm it is in the tree before the change, then use NVDA's speech viewer or VoiceOver's caption panel to see exactly what is spoken.

questions.q: How would you make a toast notification system accessible?
questions.answer:
**Render toasts inside persistent live regions (polite for confirmations, assertive only for urgent errors), never move focus to them, keep them visible long enough and pause dismissal on hover and focus, make any action reachable by keyboard or available elsewhere, and never let a toast be the only place important information or actions exist.**

## Why toasts are hard
- They appear far from focus, so screen reader users miss them unless announced.
- They vanish on a timer, possibly before a screen reader finishes speaking or before a magnifier user pans to them (2.2.1 Timing Adjustable).
- Their actions ("Undo") are often unreachable before they disappear.
- Several at once compete for attention.

## Design
```text
App root
 |- ToastViewport (region "Notifications", reachable via F8-style hotkey)
 |    polite live region  <- "Message archived" [Undo]
 |    assertive region    <- "Could not send. Retry?"
 |- page content keeps focus
```
1. **Announcement**: the viewport is mounted once; toasts append text into a polite live region (`role="status"`). Errors that block the user go to `role="alert"`. Message text is complete on its own: "Invoice INV-1043 deleted", not "Done".
2. **No focus theft**: focus stays where the user is working.
3. **Timing**: auto-dismiss after enough time to read (often 5 to 10 seconds, longer for longer text), pause on hover and on focus within, and do not auto-dismiss toasts that contain actions, or make that configurable.
4. **Reachable actions**: a documented hotkey to jump to the notification region (Radix Toast uses F8 by default), and the same action available in the main UI (Undo also in the item menu or a "Recently deleted" view).
5. **Persistence of information**: the outcome is also visible in the page (the row disappears, a status badge changes). A notification centre can keep history.
6. **Motion**: slide-in animations respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
7. **Stacking**: queue or collapse multiple toasts ("3 files uploaded") instead of announcing each.
8. **Contrast and target size**: text 4.5:1, close button at least 24 by 24 CSS px with a name ("Dismiss notification").

## When not to use a toast
If the user must decide something now ("Discard unsaved changes?") or a failure blocks progress, use a `role="alertdialog"` that takes focus, or an inline error next to the relevant content. Toasts are for non-critical confirmations.

## Testing
Trigger each toast type with NVDA and VoiceOver running: it should be announced once, not interrupt typing (polite), be reachable via the hotkey, and stay while focused. Axe checks contrast and names; only listening checks the rest.

questions.q: What contrast ratios does WCAG require, and how do you build them into a design system?
questions.answer:
**At Level AA, normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background and large text at least 3:1 (1.4.3); user interface component boundaries, states and meaningful graphics need 3:1 (1.4.11). AAA raises text to 7:1 and 4.5:1. In a design system you encode verified pairs as tokens and test them automatically for every theme.**

## The numbers
| What | Level | Ratio |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body text | AA | 4.5:1 |
| Large text (24 CSS px regular, or about 18.66 px bold) | AA | 3:1 |
| Input borders, checkbox outlines, focus indicators, toggle states, chart lines, meaningful icons | AA (1.4.11) | 3:1 against adjacent colours |
| Body text | AAA (1.4.6) | 7:1 |
| Large text | AAA | 4.5:1 |
Exempt: disabled controls, purely decorative elements, logos, incidental text in photos.

The ratio comes from relative luminance: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), from 1:1 to 21:1. Typical traps: `#767676` on white is about 4.5:1 (the lightest grey that passes); `#999` is about 2.8:1; many brand oranges and greens land between 3:1 and 4.5:1, fine for big headings, failing for body text.

## Building it in
```css
:root {
  --text: #1f2430;            /* about 15:1 on white */
  --text-muted: #5b6270;      /* about 6:1, safe for secondary text */
  --border-input: #7a808c;    /* >= 3:1 for 1.4.11 */
  --focus-ring: #2a5bd7;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
  --text: #e8eaf0;
  --text-muted: #a6adbb;
  --border-input: #8a92a3;
}
```
1. **Tokens define pairs**, not just colours: `text-muted` on `surface`, `on-primary` on `primary`. Document allowed combinations.
2. **Automated checks** on the token build: compute every declared pair and fail CI under threshold. Then axe in Storybook and Playwright catches real rendered combinations, including dark mode.
3. **States**: hover, focus, selected, error and visited states are checked too, not only the default.
4. **Text over imagery**: require a scrim or solid background in the component, not ad-hoc.
5. **Forced colours**: use real borders and outlines so Windows high-contrast mode still shows component boundaries.

## APCA
The Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm was developed as a candidate for WCAG 3 and models perception better (especially dark mode and thin fonts). It is not part of WCAG 2.x, and WCAG 3 is still a draft, so for conformance in 2026 you measure the WCAG 2 ratio; APCA can inform design choices on top.

## Tools
WebAIM Contrast Checker, Chrome DevTools colour picker (shows ratio and AA/AAA lines), axe and Lighthouse for rendered pages.

questions.q: How do you write good alt text, and when should alt be empty?
questions.answer:
**Alt text should convey the information or function the image provides in its context, as concisely as the surrounding text allows. Use an empty `alt=""` when the image is decorative or its information is already in adjacent text, so screen readers skip it; never omit the attribute, because screen readers may then read the file name.**

## Decision process (after the W3C WAI alt decision tree)
```text
Image is the only content of a link/button?  -> describe the destination/action
Image contains text?                          -> the same text
Image adds information not in nearby text?    -> short description of that info
Image is decorative or duplicates nearby text -> alt=""
Complex image (chart, diagram, map)?          -> short alt + long description
                                                 nearby (data table, summary)
```

## Examples
| Context | Good alt |
| --- | --- |
| Logo linking to the home page | "Acme home" |
| Magnifier icon in a search button | "Search" |
| Product photo on product page | "Navy wool coat, front view, knee length" |
| Same photo in cart row next to the product name | "" |
| Author headshot next to the author's name | "" |
| Line chart in an article | "Monthly active users, Jan to Jun 2026, rising from 40k to 95k" plus a data table |
| Screenshot illustrating an error | The error text and what it shows that matters |
| Decorative divider or background flourish | "" (or use CSS background) |

## Rules of thumb
- **Context changes the answer**: the same image can need different alt on different pages.
- **Do not start with "Image of" or "Picture of"**; the role is announced. "Photo of" or "Illustration of" is acceptable when the medium itself matters.
- **Be concise**: usually a short sentence. Long descriptions go in visible text or a linked description.
- **Do not duplicate captions**: if a figure caption already says it, alt can be shorter or empty.
- **Inline SVG**: decorative gets `aria-hidden="true"`; meaningful gets `role="img"` and `aria-label`.
- **Frameworks**: Next.js `Image` requires `alt`; pass `""` deliberately for decoration.

## User-generated and AI alt text
Let users add alt text when they upload (many social platforms prompt for it) and fall back to an empty alt rather than the file name. AI-generated descriptions can draft alt text, but they describe what is visible, not why the author included it, and can be wrong; treat them as an editable suggestion and label them as automatic if shown.

## Process
Alt text is editorial work. Engineering makes it mandatory (CMS required field with an explicit "decorative" checkbox, `jsx-a11y/alt-text` lint rule, axe checks for missing alt) and reviews it in content QA.

questions.q: Why should colour never be the only way to convey information, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
**WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color (A) says colour cannot be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response or distinguishing an element. Colour vision deficiencies are common, colour is lost in monochrome displays and forced-colours modes, and screen readers do not announce colour. Pair colour with text, icons, shapes, patterns or underlines.**

## Who is affected
Roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some colour vision deficiency, most often red-green. Add low vision, sunlight glare on mobile screens, cheap projectors, grayscale printing and Windows high-contrast themes that replace your palette entirely.

## Fixes by pattern
| Colour-only version | Accessible version |
| --- | --- |
| Invalid field has a red border | Red border + error icon + text "Enter a valid postcode", `aria-invalid` |
| Status dots: green, amber, red | Dot + text label ("Healthy", "Degraded", "Down") or distinct shapes (check, triangle, cross) |
| Links distinguished only by colour in a paragraph | Underline (simplest), or 3:1 contrast with surrounding text plus an underline on hover and focus |
| Line chart with series by colour | Direct labels at line ends, different markers or dash patterns, plus a data table |
| Required fields shown in red | "(required)" text, or an asterisk explained at the top |
| Selected tab shown only by colour | Underline bar or weight change plus `aria-selected` |
| Calendar availability by colour | Text or icon in each cell, and an accessible name like "12 June, available" |

## Screen readers
Colour does not reach the accessibility tree. The equivalent of "red means error" is a state (`aria-invalid`), a role, or text. For status badges, the text is the meaning; colour reinforces it.

## Contrast is a separate criterion
A red-green pair can have perfect contrast against the background and still be indistinguishable from each other for someone with deuteranopia. 1.4.1 and 1.4.3/1.4.11 are both needed.

## Testing
Chrome DevTools Rendering panel can emulate protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, achromatopsia and blurred vision. Switching a screenshot to grayscale is a quick sanity check: if you can still tell every state apart, you pass the spirit of 1.4.1. Automated tools cannot detect colour-only meaning reliably; this is a design review and manual check.

questions.q: How do you make data tables and charts accessible?
questions.answer:
**Use a real `table` with a `caption`, `th` elements with `scope` for headers, and semantic rows so screen readers announce headers as users move between cells. For charts, give the graphic a short text summary, make series distinguishable without colour, and provide the underlying data as a table or downloadable data, since hover tooltips are not accessible on their own.** ## Tables ```tsx
Quarterly revenue by region, 2026 (USD millions)
Region Q2
EMEA 12.4 13.1
``` - Screen readers announce "EMEA, Q2, 13.1" when moving through cells with table navigation keys (Ctrl+Alt+arrows in NVDA and JAWS), which only works with real header relationships. - **Sorting**: put a `button` inside the header (not a click handler on `th`) and set `aria-sort` on the sorted column only; announce the change politely ("Sorted by Q1, descending"). - **Layout tables**: do not use tables for layout; if legacy code does, `role="presentation"` removes table semantics. - **div-based "tables"**: if you must (virtualised lists), apply `role="table"`, `row`, `columnheader`, `rowheader`, `cell` consistently, plus `aria-rowcount` and `aria-rowindex` for virtualised rows. - **role="grid"** is for interactive spreadsheets with arrow-key cell navigation and editable cells (APG grid pattern). Most data tables are not grids; adding the role puts screen readers into an application mode with different expectations. - **Responsiveness**: 1.4.10 Reflow exempts content that needs two-dimensional layout, like data tables, but you can still put the table in a horizontally scrollable region (`tabindex="0"`, `role="region"`, `aria-labelledby` the caption) so keyboard users can scroll it. ## Charts 1. **Summary**: a text alternative stating the takeaway ("Revenue grew 18% quarter on quarter, led by EMEA"). For SVG charts, `role="img"` with `aria-labelledby` pointing at a visible title and summary. 2. **Data access**: a visible or toggleable data table, or CSV download. This is the single most valuable step. 3. **Not colour alone**: direct labels, markers, dash patterns; lines and bars 3:1 against the background (1.4.11). 4. **Interactive charts**: if points are focusable, each needs a name ("June: 95,000 users") and keyboard navigation; tooltips must appear on focus and follow 1.4.13 (dismissible, hoverable, persistent). 5. **Motion**: chart entrance animations respect reduced motion. Libraries differ widely: Highcharts has a dedicated accessibility module with keyboard navigation and sonification; many lightweight libraries output unlabelled SVG. Evaluate before choosing. ## Testing Use NVDA or VoiceOver table navigation to confirm header announcements; axe checks for headers without data and missing captions; review the chart with a screen reader to ensure the summary and data are reachable.
followUps: When should you use role="grid" instead of a plain table?

Weak answers rely on a chart's colours and tooltips as the only way to read data.
Weak answers add role="grid" to every table, forcing an interaction model users did not need.

questions.q: How do you test a web app for accessibility, and what can automated tools not catch?
questions.answer:
**I use layers: lint rules and typed component APIs, axe-core in component, Storybook and end-to-end tests, Testing Library role queries, then manual keyboard, zoom and screen reader checks, plus periodic audits and sessions with disabled users. Automated tools catch only part of WCAG issues; they cannot judge meaning, focus flow, announcement quality or whether a task is actually usable.**

## The layers
```text
lint (eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y) + required label props in TS
 -> unit/component: vitest-axe / jest-axe + getByRole queries
 -> Storybook a11y addon (axe per story, themes)
 -> Playwright + @axe-core/playwright on key flows, in interactive states
 -> manual: keyboard-only, 200%/400% zoom, reduced motion, forced colours
 -> screen readers: NVDA + Firefox/Chrome, VoiceOver + Safari (macOS, iOS)
 -> periodic external audit (WCAG 2.2 AA, ACR) + user testing
```

## Playwright example
```ts
test("checkout errors are accessible", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/checkout");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Pay now" }).click(); // trigger error state
  await expect(page.getByRole("heading", { name: "There is a problem" })).toBeFocused();
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(["wcag2a", "wcag2aa", "wcag22aa"]).analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});
```
Scan the states that matter: menus open, dialogs open, forms with errors, dark mode. The initial load is a small part of the app.

## What automation catches well
Missing names on buttons, links and inputs; missing alt attributes; contrast (in a real browser); invalid ARIA attributes and roles; missing page language; duplicate ids in ARIA references; positive tabindex; some landmark and heading structure problems. Deque reports that axe finds roughly 57% of issues by volume in its audit data; the UK GDS 2017 experiment with deliberately planted barriers found every tool missed a large share. Either way, it is a floor.

## What it cannot catch
- Whether alt text, labels and headings are **meaningful** (alt="image" passes).
- **Focus order and focus management**: focus lost after deleting a row, dialog not returning focus.
- **Keyboard operability** of custom widgets (a `div` with a click handler and `role="button"` but no key handler may pass).
- **Announcements**: missing, duplicated or interrupting live region messages.
- **Colour-only meaning**, reflow and zoom problems, motion issues.
- **Cognitive load and usability**: confusing flows, timeouts, jargon.

## Rolling it into CI
Lint and component axe tests block merges. E2E axe on critical journeys blocks release. For a legacy app with many existing violations, record a baseline, fail only on new violations, and burn down by rule, starting with shared components. Every excluded rule or element needs an owner and a reason.

## Manual checks I expect per feature
Tab through without a mouse, operate everything, zoom to 400%, toggle reduced motion and forced colours, and do a short screen reader pass of the main task.

questions.q: How do you test with a screen reader, and which screen reader and browser pairings do you use?
questions.answer:
**I test the pairings screen readers are built for and that most users have: NVDA with Firefox or Chrome on Windows, VoiceOver with Safari on macOS and iOS, and TalkBack with Chrome on Android; JAWS with Chrome too for enterprise or government products. I navigate the way users do (headings, landmarks, the virtual cursor, then Tab through controls) and check roles, names, states, announcements and focus movement.**

## Pairings and essentials
| Pairing | Start | Core keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVDA + Firefox/Chrome | Free download | NVDA key = Insert or Caps Lock. Down arrow next item, H headings, D landmarks, F form fields, K links, Tab controls, NVDA+F7 elements list, NVDA+Space browse/focus toggle, Ctrl stop speech |
| VoiceOver + Safari (macOS) | Cmd+F5 | VO = Ctrl+Option. VO+Right next item, VO+U rotor (headings, links, landmarks, form controls), VO+Space activate |
| VoiceOver + Safari (iOS) | Accessibility shortcut (triple-click) | Swipe right/left next/previous, double-tap activate, two-finger twist for rotor |
| TalkBack + Chrome (Android) | Volume keys shortcut | Swipe to move, double-tap activate, reading controls |

WebAIM's screen reader user survey consistently shows JAWS and NVDA dominate desktop use and VoiceOver dominates mobile, and that most users navigate unfamiliar pages by headings first.

## Browse mode and focus mode
On Windows, NVDA and JAWS run a **browse mode** (virtual cursor) where single keys navigate the page (H for heading). When the user reaches a text field or a widget with an application-type role, they switch to **focus mode** and pass keys to the page. This explains "it works with Tab but not with NVDA" bugs: a custom widget without correct roles may never trigger focus mode, so arrow keys move the virtual cursor instead of your widget.

## A repeatable script
```text
1. Page load: title announced? Language correct (pronunciation)?
2. Headings (H / rotor): logical outline, one h1, meaningful text?
3. Landmarks (D / rotor): main, nav (named if several), banner, contentinfo?
4. Tab through controls: role, name, state correct? ("Filters, button, collapsed")
5. Operate: expanded/checked/selected changes announced?
6. Dynamic updates: status messages announced exactly once?
7. Forms: submit empty; can you find and fix each error by ear?
8. Dialogs: name announced on open, focus contained, returned on close?
9. Images: meaningful alt read, decorative skipped?
```
Turn the monitor off or close your eyes for part of it; otherwise you navigate by sight.

## Tooling
NVDA's speech viewer prints everything spoken, which is ideal for bug reports ("expected: Delete invoice, button; actual: button"). VoiceOver has a caption panel. Record the screen reader, version, browser and OS in every bug, because behaviour differs across combinations.

## Limits of developer testing
Developers are novice screen reader users and miss what fluent users find, and fluent users find workarounds developers would not. Periodic sessions with experienced assistive tech users catch both.

questions.q: How would you roll out accessibility across a large existing codebase and team that has ignored it?
questions.answer:
**Fix at the source and stop the bleeding: commit to WCAG 2.2 AA, make shared components accessible first, baseline automated violations and fail CI only on new ones, add accessibility to the definition of done, then burn down issues by user impact on critical journeys, with periodic audits to measure real progress.**

## Phase 1: assess cheaply (weeks 1 to 2)
- Run axe across key routes in their main states (Playwright crawl) to get a baseline grouped by rule and by component.
- Manually test the top 3 to 5 user journeys (sign-up, checkout, core task) with keyboard and one screen reader. These reveal blockers automation cannot see.
- Most violations cluster in a few shared components: one fix to `IconButton` or `Select` can clear hundreds of nodes.

## Phase 2: stop regressions
- `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` in warn mode, then error mode for new files.
- axe in CI with a **baseline**: known violations recorded, new ones fail. No team gets blocked by legacy debt.
- Component API changes: required `label` on icon buttons, dialogs that require a title, a `Field` component that wires labels and errors.
- Definition of done: keyboard pass and axe clean for touched screens; designers annotate focus order, headings and names in specs.

## Phase 3: fix at the source
- Rebuild or replace the riskiest primitives (menus, comboboxes, dialogs, date pickers) with a vetted headless library such as React Aria or Radix.
- Fix design tokens for contrast once; every screen benefits.
- Add skip links, landmarks, page titles and route focus management in the app shell.

## Phase 4: burn down by impact
Severity by user impact, not count:
```text
Blocker  : cannot complete a critical task (keyboard trap in checkout,
           unlabelled payment fields)            -> fix this sprint
Critical : major difficulty on key flows          -> next sprint
Serious  : workaround exists                      -> scheduled
Minor    : annoyance / best practice              -> opportunistic
```
Accessibility bugs live in the normal backlog with owners and SLAs.

## People and process
- A small champions network (one engineer and designer per team) with training and office hours.
- Short training on keyboard and screen reader basics for every engineer; it changes behaviour more than documentation.
- Publish an accessibility statement and a feedback channel; triage user reports quickly.
- External audit annually or before major releases to produce an ACR for sales.

## Measuring progress
Violations per page over time, the share of key journeys passing manual checks, time-to-fix for blockers, coverage of component tests with axe, and qualitative results from user testing. Violation counts alone can be gamed by excluding rules.

questions.q: How would you build an accessible combobox or autocomplete?
questions.answer:
**First check whether a native `select` or `datalist` is enough; if not, use a tested library like React Aria. The ARIA 1.2 pattern puts `role="combobox"` on the input with `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` and `aria-autocomplete`, the popup is a `listbox` of `option`s, DOM focus stays in the input and `aria-activedescendant` points at the highlighted option. Down and Up move, Enter selects, Escape closes, and result counts are announced politely.** ## Structure ```text
  • Berlin
  • Bern
2 suggestions
``` ## Keyboard model (APG) | Key | Behaviour | | --- | --- | | Typing | Filters options; focus stays in input | | Down | Opens popup and/or moves highlight to the next option | | Up | Previous option | | Alt+Down | Opens without moving highlight | | Enter | Accepts highlighted option, closes popup | | Escape | Closes popup; a second Escape may clear the input | | Home/End | Move the caret in the input (standard text editing) | ## Why aria-activedescendant The user must keep typing, so real focus cannot leave the input. The screen reader announces the referenced option ("Bern, 2 of 2"). Your responsibilities: keep option ids stable and rendered, scroll the highlighted option into view, style it visibly (no `:focus` on it), and clear `aria-activedescendant` when nothing is highlighted. ## Async and edge cases - Debounce requests; show a visible loading row and announce "Loading suggestions" only if slow, then "5 suggestions" or "No results". - Ignore stale responses (abort or compare request ids) so a slow earlier response does not overwrite newer results. - Distinguish **free text** from **must choose**: on blur, does an unmatched value stay or revert? Communicate that in the label or hint. - Multi-select: selected items as removable tokens, each a button named "Remove Berlin". - Mobile: the virtual keyboard covers the list; limit list height and test with VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack. ## History ARIA 1.0 and 1.1 had different structures (1.1 put the combobox role on a wrapper containing a textbox). ARIA 1.2 simplified it to the role on the input itself; older libraries may still use the old structure, which some screen readers handle poorly. ## Build or buy React Aria's `useComboBox`, Downshift, Ariakit and Headless UI implement this with years of cross-screen-reader fixes. Unless the product needs something unusual, wrap one of them, require a `label` prop, and spend your time testing rather than re-implementing.
followUps: How would you handle async suggestions and loading?
What changed between the ARIA 1.1 and 1.2 combobox patterns?
When is a native select or datalist enough?
mistakes: Weak answers move DOM focus into the list, so typing breaks.
Weak answers forget to announce the number of results or the loading state.
Weak answers build it from scratch without testing on VoiceOver and NVDA, where support differs.

questions.q: What does the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide recommend for an accessible tabs component?
questions.answer:
**A tab list has `role="tablist"` with a name; each tab is `role="tab"` with `aria-selected` and `aria-controls` pointing at its `role="tabpanel"`, and each panel is labelled by its tab. The tab list is a single Tab stop using roving tabindex: arrow keys move between tabs, Home and End jump to the ends, and Tab moves into the active panel. Activation is automatic or manual depending on how expensive panels are.** ## Markup ```tsx
...
...
``` Screen readers announce "Account settings, tab list, Profile, tab, selected, 1 of 2". ## Keyboard | Key | Action | | --- | --- | | Tab | Into the tab list (lands on the selected tab), then into the panel | | Left / Right | Previous / next tab (wrapping) | | Up / Down | Same, for `aria-orientation="vertical"` tab lists | | Home / End | First / last tab | | Enter / Space | Activate (manual activation mode) | | Delete | Optional: close a deletable tab | ## Automatic versus manual activation - **Automatic**: moving to a tab shows its panel immediately. Best when panels are already rendered or cheap. - **Manual**: arrows only move focus; Enter or Space activates. Best when showing a panel triggers network requests or heavy rendering, so users arrowing past do not load every panel. ## Panel details - `tabIndex={0}` on the panel when it has no focusable content, so keyboard users can reach it and scroll it; omit it when the first focusable element inside is enough. - Hidden panels use `hidden` (removed from the tree), not just `opacity: 0`. ## When it is not tabs If each "tab" has its own URL and loads a new page or route, it is navigation: a `nav` with links and `aria-current="page"` on the current one. Using the tab role there changes the screen reader interaction model and promises arrow keys that conflict with links. ## Implementation React Aria `useTabList`, Radix Tabs and Headless UI Tab implement this, including the activation modes and orientation. Test that arrow keys work in NVDA focus mode and with VoiceOver on macOS.
followUps: When should tabs be links instead?
What happens to the panel's tab order?
How do vertical tabs differ?
mistakes: Weak answers make every tab a separate Tab stop.
Weak answers use the tab pattern for page navigation that changes the URL.
Weak answers forget aria-selected and aria-controls or leave hidden panels in the tree.

questions.q: Should a site navigation dropdown use the ARIA menu role?
questions.answer:
**Usually no. The ARIA `menu` role models an application-style command menu, like a desktop app's File menu, with arrow-key navigation and a different screen reader interaction mode. A website navigation dropdown is a list of links, best built as a disclosure: a button with `aria-expanded` that shows a list of ordinary links, which users move through with Tab.** ## Why the menu role is a poor fit for navigation - **Interaction model**: `menu` and `menuitem` promise arrow keys, type-ahead, Escape behaviour and a single Tab stop. Users visiting a website expect links reachable with Tab. - **Screen reader behaviour**: inside a `menu`, Windows screen readers switch to focus/application handling, and items are announced as menu items, not links. Users lose link-specific features such as the links list and "open in new tab" expectations. - **Content restrictions**: menus can only contain menu items (and groups and separators). Mega-menus with headings, descriptions and images break the pattern. - **Maintenance**: hand-built menus are a frequent source of bugs (missing keyboard support, focus not returned), producing worse results than plain links. ## The disclosure navigation pattern (APG example "Disclosure Navigation Menu") ```tsx
    • Analytics
    • Billing
  • Pricing
``` Behaviour: - Click, Enter or Space toggles; Escape closes and returns focus to the button. - Tab moves through the links naturally; closing when focus leaves the group is a common enhancement. - Hover can also open it for mouse users, but never only hover; and follow 1.4.13 (hover content must be hoverable and dismissible). - The trigger is a button (it toggles), unless the top level is itself a link, in which case add a separate small toggle button next to it. ## When role="menu" is right Application-style action menus: a "More actions" kebab menu in a data table, an editor's Format menu, a context menu. Pattern: menu button (`aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded`) opening a `menu` of `menuitem`, `menuitemcheckbox` or `menuitemradio` with full APG keyboard support. Libraries like Radix DropdownMenu and React Aria `useMenu` implement this. ## Summary Navigation: disclosure plus links. Commands: menu button plus menu. Choosing by appearance ("it drops down") rather than purpose is the root of the mistake.

questions.q: Would you build accessible components yourself or use a headless library like Radix or React Aria?
questions.answer:
**For complex widgets (combobox, menu, dialog, date picker, grid, tabs) I would use a well-tested headless library and wrap it in our design system with APIs that require accessible names. For simple things (buttons, disclosures, toggles) I would use native elements directly. A library handles behaviour and ARIA, but we still own labelling, focus styles, content and testing.**

## Why buy for complex widgets
Getting a combobox right means handling `aria-activedescendant`, virtual keyboards, IME composition, RTL, touch screen readers, scroll into view, and dozens of screen reader and browser quirks. Library maintainers have already absorbed years of those bug reports. Rebuilding that is months of specialist work with a high chance of subtle failures.

## The options
| Library | Character |
| --- | --- |
| React Aria / React Aria Components (Adobe) | Hooks plus components; very thorough testing across screen readers and touch, internationalisation, drag-and-drop with accessible alternatives |
| Radix Primitives | Unstyled components, widely used via shadcn/ui; follows APG patterns; strong focus management |
| Headless UI | Smaller set, simple API, React and Vue |
| Ariakit | Low-level composable primitives, strong on correctness |
| Downshift | Focused on combobox/select |
| Native | `dialog`, `details`, `popover`, `select` (including the newer customisable select where supported) |

## How to evaluate
- Does the documentation state which APG pattern each component follows and which screen readers and browsers are tested?
- Read open issues tagged accessibility: are they addressed?
- Run your own quick NVDA and VoiceOver (macOS and iOS) check of the components you need.
- Check keyboard support tables against the APG.

## What can still go wrong
- Missing names: a `Dialog` without a `Title`, icon-only triggers without labels. (Radix warns in development for missing dialog titles.)
- Breaking composition: wrapping triggers in extra elements, nesting a button inside a button, or forgetting `asChild`.
- Overriding behaviour: custom focus handlers, `onOpenAutoFocus` prevented without an alternative.
- Styling: removing focus rings, low-contrast states, tiny targets.
- Content: unclear labels, missing error text.

## Wrapping in a design system
```tsx
type SelectProps<T> = {
  label: string;                 // required accessible name
  hint?: string;
  error?: string;
  options: { value: T; label: string }[];
  value: T | null;
  onChange: (v: T) => void;
};
```
The wrapper wires label, hint and error ids, applies token-based focus and contrast styles, and does not expose props that break the pattern. Storybook stories document the keyboard model, and axe plus keyboard tests run on every story.

## Trade-offs
Bundle size and API lock-in (mitigated by wrapping), styling constraints, and upgrade churn. Against that, the cost of shipping an inaccessible combobox to every product team is much higher.
